definitions.definition: A fancy word for when two things have the same structure or pattern, even if they look different on the surface.
definitions.example: A map of a subway system and the actual subway tracks are isomorphic because the connections between stations are the same.

definitions.definition: How well things fit together in a logical or meaningful way, like pieces of a puzzle that match.
definitions.example: If your story has no contradictions and makes sense from start to finish, it has high coherence.

definitions.definition: A method where you try to find flaws or weaknesses in an idea, like a lawyer arguing against it, to test how strong it really is.
definitions.example: In a debate, one person argues for an idea and the other argues against it to see which side is stronger.

definitions.definition: Separate areas or fields of knowledge or experience.
definitions.example: Math and music are different domains, but both use patterns.

definitions.definition: A measure of disorder or randomness in a system; things tend to get messier over time unless energy is used to keep them organized.
definitions.example: Your bedroom gets messier on its own (entropy increases) unless you clean it.

definitions.definition: Equations that describe how things change over time or space, using rates of change.
definitions.example: Predicting how fast a ball will fall or how a disease spreads uses differential equations.

definitions.definition: A way of pairing up items from one set with items from another set so that each item has a partner.
definitions.example: Matching students to their desks in a classroom is a mapping.

definitions.definition: Relating to the way parts are arranged or connected, not just the surface details.
definitions.example: Two different buildings can be structurally similar if they have the same frame, even if one is brick and the other is wood.

definitions.definition: A way to measure how surprising or unlikely a piece of information is, based on how many yes/no questions you'd need to guess it.
definitions.example: If someone tells you the exact card you picked from a deck, that's about 5.7 bits of information because you'd need that many yes/no questions to guess it.

definitions.definition: The smallest unit of information, like a single yes or no answer.
definitions.example: A light switch being on or off stores 1 bit of information.

definitions.definition: A way of updating your belief about something based on new evidence, using math to calculate how likely it is.
definitions.example: If you hear thunder, Bayesian analysis helps you update how likely you think rain is.

definitions.definition: The simplest explanation that requires the fewest steps or rules to describe something.
definitions.example: If you see a wet sidewalk, the Kolmogorov-minimal explanation is that it rained, not that someone spilled a million buckets.

definitions.definition: When a quantum system loses its special connectedness and starts acting like normal, everyday objects.
definitions.example: Think of two dancers moving perfectly together, then one trips and they fall out of sync — that's like decoherence.

definitions.definition: A way of mapping out cause-and-effect relationships, like a flowchart showing what leads to what.
definitions.example: A diagram showing that smoking causes lung cancer, which causes coughing, is a simple causal inference network.

definitions.definition: A problem that can be solved or analyzed using clear math or logic, not just guesswork.
definitions.example: Adding two numbers is formally tractable; guessing someone's favorite color is not.

definitions.definition: The maximum amount of information that can be sent reliably through a communication link, like a wire or radio wave.
definitions.example: A water pipe has a maximum flow rate; channel capacity is the same idea for information.

definitions.definition: Lying under oath in a court of law.
definitions.example: If you swear to tell the truth in court and then lie, that's perjury.

definitions.definition: A set of rules to make sure a message is sent and received without errors or corruption.
definitions.example: When you text someone, the phone uses a signal integrity protocol to make sure 'hello' doesn't become 'h3llo'.
